content.title: Complex sentences: combining with relative, adverbial and noun clauses
content.instructions: Combine the sentences into ONE sentence using the structure given in brackets. Keep the original meaning, remove any words that become unnecessary, and punctuate carefully (non-defining relative clauses need commas).

items.prompt: Norway had the highest proportion of electric car sales in 2020. Its government offers generous tax incentives to buyers. (non-defining relative clause with 'whose')
accepted_answers: Norway, whose government offers generous tax incentives to buyers, had the highest proportion of electric car sales in 2020.
items.model_answer: Norway, whose government offers generous tax incentives to buyers, had the highest proportion of electric car sales in 2020.
items.explanation: 'Whose' replaces a possessive (its, their, his) and links it to the noun before it. Because 'Norway' is already fully identified, the clause is non-defining and must be enclosed in commas.

items.prompt: Some students study abroad. These students often return with valuable language skills. (defining relative clause with 'who')
accepted_answers: Students who study abroad often return with valuable language skills.
The students who study abroad often return with valuable language skills.
items.model_answer: Students who study abroad often return with valuable language skills.
items.explanation: A defining relative clause identifies which people we mean (only those who study abroad), so it takes no commas. Adding commas would wrongly suggest that all students study abroad.

items.prompt: Many people move to big cities. They want better-paid jobs. (adverbial clause of reason)
accepted_answers: Many people move to big cities because they want better-paid jobs.
Many people move to big cities as they want better-paid jobs.
As they want better-paid jobs, many people move to big cities.
Since they want better-paid jobs, many people move to big cities.
items.model_answer: Many people move to big cities because they want better-paid jobs.
items.explanation: Reason clauses are introduced by because, as or since. When the subordinate clause comes first, put a comma after it; when it comes second, no comma is usually needed after 'because'.

items.prompt: Online learning is much cheaper. Many employers still prefer traditional degrees. (concession clause with 'although')
accepted_answers: Although online learning is much cheaper, many employers still prefer traditional degrees.
Many employers still prefer traditional degrees, although online learning is much cheaper.
items.model_answer: Although online learning is much cheaper, many employers still prefer traditional degrees.
items.explanation: 'Although' introduces a contrast that you concede before making your main point. Never combine it with 'but' in the same sentence ('Although …, but …' is a typical band-5 error).

items.prompt: Sales of laptops fell in 2019. Sales of tablets rose in the same year. (contrast clause with 'whereas' or 'while')
accepted_answers: Sales of laptops fell in 2019, whereas sales of tablets rose in the same year.
Sales of laptops fell in 2019, while sales of tablets rose in the same year.
Whereas sales of laptops fell in 2019, sales of tablets rose in the same year.
While sales of laptops fell in 2019, sales of tablets rose in the same year.
items.model_answer: While sales of laptops fell in 2019, sales of tablets rose in the same year.
items.explanation: 'Whereas' and 'while' join two contrasting facts in one sentence, which is ideal for Task 1 comparisons. A comma separates the two clauses in either order.

items.prompt: The survey was conducted in 2022. It asked 2,000 adults about their reading habits. (non-defining relative clause with 'which')
accepted_answers: The survey, which was conducted in 2022, asked 2,000 adults about their reading habits.
The survey, which asked 2,000 adults about their reading habits, was conducted in 2022.
items.model_answer: The survey, which was conducted in 2022, asked 2,000 adults about their reading habits.
items.explanation: A non-defining clause adds extra information about something already identified (the survey). It uses 'which' (never 'that') and is separated from the main clause by a pair of commas.

items.prompt: Nobody knows the answer to this question. Will remote working remain popular over the next decade? (noun clause with 'whether')
accepted_answers: Nobody knows whether remote working will remain popular over the next decade.
Nobody knows whether or not remote working will remain popular over the next decade.
items.model_answer: Nobody knows whether remote working will remain popular over the next decade.
items.explanation: When a yes/no question becomes a noun clause, it is introduced by 'whether' (or 'if') and uses statement word order: subject + verb (remote working will remain), not question order (will remote working remain), and it has no question mark.

items.prompt: Most tourists visited the coastal region. Hotel prices there were the lowest in the country. (relative clause with 'where')
accepted_answers: Most tourists visited the coastal region, where hotel prices were the lowest in the country.
items.model_answer: Most tourists visited the coastal region, where hotel prices were the lowest in the country.
items.explanation: 'Where' replaces 'there' / 'in that place' and introduces a relative clause about a place. Do not keep 'there' inside the clause ('where hotel prices there were …' repeats the place).

items.prompt: The factory closed in 2015. Soon afterwards, unemployment in the town rose sharply. (time clause with 'after' or 'once')
accepted_answers: After the factory closed in 2015, unemployment in the town rose sharply.
Unemployment in the town rose sharply after the factory closed in 2015.
Once the factory closed in 2015, unemployment in the town rose sharply.
items.model_answer: After the factory closed in 2015, unemployment in the town rose sharply.
items.explanation: A time clause (after, once, when, as soon as) shows the sequence of two events in one sentence. Put a comma after the time clause when it comes first.

items.prompt: Many cities have built cycle lanes. They want more residents to leave their cars at home. (purpose clause with 'so that')
accepted_answers: Many cities have built cycle lanes so that more residents will leave their cars at home.
Many cities have built cycle lanes so that more residents leave their cars at home.
Many cities have built cycle lanes so that more residents can leave their cars at home.
items.model_answer: Many cities have built cycle lanes so that more residents will leave their cars at home.
items.explanation: 'So that' introduces a purpose clause with its own subject (more residents), usually followed by will/can/could. Use 'to' or 'in order to' only when the subject of both clauses is the same.
